headings.title: Role of Gloves in Infection Prevention
headings.content: Gloves act as a physical barrier to prevent the transmission of microorganisms between healthcare workers and patients. They protect hands from coming into contact with blood, body fluids, mucous membranes, and non-intact skin. Wearing gloves does not replace the need for hand hygiene. Microbes can rapidly multiply on the warm, moist skin inside gloves, making handwashing mandatory immediately after glove removal. Nurses must recognize that gloves are single-use items designed for specific tasks and must never be washed or reused.

headings.title: Indications for Wearing Gloves
headings.content:
Clinical judgment dictates when gloves are required. Nurses wear them whenever contact with blood, body fluids, secretions, excretions, and contaminated items is anticipated. 

- **Direct Patient Care**: Venipuncture, insertion of urinary catheters, oral care, and handling wounds.
- **Indirect Patient Care**: Emptying drainage containers, handling soiled linen, and cleaning contaminated equipment.

Gloves are unnecessary for routine care tasks that do not involve potential fluid exposure, such as feeding a stable patient, taking a blood pressure over intact skin, or distributing oral medications.

headings.title: Examination versus Surgical Gloves
headings.content:
Selecting the correct category of gloves depends entirely on the nature of the procedure being performed in the ward or theatre.

| Feature | Examination Gloves | Surgical Gloves |
|---|---|---|>
| **Sterility** | Non-sterile (clean) | Sterile |
| **Sizing** | General sizes (S, M, L) | Exact sizing (5.5 to 9.0) |
| **Primary Use** | Routine care, exams, labs | Invasive procedures, surgery |

headings.title: Material Selection: Latex, Nitrile, and Vinyl
headings.content:
Gloves are manufactured from various materials to accommodate patient and staff allergies, chemical exposures, and task demands.

- **Natural Rubber Latex**: Offers superior fit, comfort, and tactile sensitivity, but poses a severe risk of IgE-mediated allergic reactions for sensitive staff and patients.
- **Nitrile**: Made from synthetic copolymer, providing high puncture resistance and chemical protection. It is the preferred alternative for latex-allergic individuals.
- **Vinyl**: A synthetic plastic material that is cost-effective and latex-free, but lacks the elasticity and durability of nitrile or latex. It tears easily and is reserved for short, low-risk tasks.

headings.title: Proper Glove Donning Technique
headings.content: Putting on gloves correctly ensures the barrier remains intact before touching a patient. Perform hand hygiene thoroughly before touching any gloves. Inspect the packaging for tears or moisture. Pull the glove over the hand, making sure the cuff covers the wrist of the isolation gown if one is worn. Avoid touching unneeded surfaces or adjusting the mask and hair once the clean or sterile gloves are on. If a glove tears during a task, stop immediately, remove both gloves, perform hand hygiene, and put on a fresh pair.

headings.title: Safe Removal and Doffing Techniques
headings.content: Taking off gloves improperly transfers trapped pathogens from the outer surface directly onto the skin of the nurse. Grasp the outside of one glove near the cuff with the opposite gloved hand and peel it away, turning it inside out as it comes off. Hold this removed glove in the palm of the remaining gloved hand. Slide the fingers of the bare hand under the wrist of the remaining glove, peeling it down over the first glove so that both are nested inside out. Discard them immediately into a medical waste bin and clean hands.

headings.title: Common Errors and Prevention of Cross-Contamination
headings.content: Improper glove habits easily spread hospital-acquired infections across the ward. A frequent mistake is wearing the same pair of gloves to care for multiple patients or touching environmental surfaces like door handles, charting clipboards, and mobile phones with contaminated gloves. Nurses must remember that gloves are patient-specific and task-specific. Never wash, disinfect, or apply alcohol rubs to disposable gloves, as chemical agents break down the barrier integrity of the material.

headings.title: Gloves within Standard and Transmission-Based Precautions
headings.content: Gloves form a core component of Tier 1 Standard Precautions applied to all hospital admissions. Beyond standard care, Transmission-Based Precautions (Contact, Droplet, Airborne) dictate specific requirements. For contact precautions—used with infections like multidrug-resistant organisms or Clostridioides difficile—gloves must be put on upon entering the room and removed before leaving. Correct disposal before exiting prevents the contamination of hospital corridors and shared equipment.
